title: Commit hygiene and release branches
description: Learn about Commit hygiene and release branches. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Commit hygiene and release branches form the backbone of a maintainable team workflow. Clean commits make debugging, reverting, and reviewing easier, while release branches give teams a safe place to prepare production-ready code.

data.title: Lesson Scope
data.text: This lesson covers commit message conventions, atomic commits, branch naming, and release branch strategies.
What Is Commit Hygiene?
Commit hygiene means keeping each commit small, focused, and well-described. A clean commit tells a clear story about what changed and why.

items: Keep commits small and logically grouped
Write descriptive subject lines
Use the body to explain motivation
Reference issue tracker IDs
Avoid mixing unrelated changes

data.text: Why Commit Hygiene Matters
Poor commit hygiene creates technical debt in version control history. Future engineers waste time deciphering vague messages, reverting huge bundles, or reconstructing intent.

items: Faster debugging with git bisect and git blame
Safer reverts without collateral damage
Easier code reviews with clear narrative
Better automated changelog generation

data.text: Atomic Commits
An atomic commit represents one logical change. If you revert it later, you lose only that change, not unrelated work. Atomic commits make cherry-picking safer and keep review focused.

items: Identify the smallest meaningful change
Stage only related files
Write a message describing only that change
Repeat for each independent modification

data.title: Partial Staging with git add -p
data.code:
git add -p src/auth/login.ts

# Git shows each hunk:
# Stage this hunk [y,n,q,a,d,e,?]? y

data.title: Amending the Most Recent Commit
data.code:
git add forgotten-file.ts

git commit --amend --no-edit

data.title: Amended Commits Change Hashes
data.text: git commit --amend rewrites the commit object. If already pushed, you must force push, which can disrupt teammates.
The Anatomy of a Great Commit Message
Most teams follow a conventional structure: a concise subject, a wrapped body explaining motivation, and a footer for metadata.

data.title: Conventional Commit Format
data.code:
feat(auth): add refresh token rotation

Rotate refresh tokens on every use to reduce the window of exposure. Store hashed tokens in the database rather than raw values.

Closes #482
BREAKING CHANGE: refresh tokens now expire after 15 minutes of inactivity.

items: Type: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore, or perf
Scope: optional module in parentheses
Subject: imperative, 50 chars or fewer
Body: wrapped at 72 chars, explain what and why
Footer: issue refs, breaking-change notices

data.text: Conventional Commits Standard
Conventional Commits is a lightweight specification. Tools like commitlint and semantic-release build on it to automate versioning and changelogs.

items: feat: a new feature
fix: a bug fix
docs: documentation only changes
style: formatting, no production code change
refactor: code change neither fixes bug nor adds feature
perf: performance improvement
test: adding or correcting tests
chore: maintenance tasks

data.title: commitlint Configuration
Creating Atomic Commits
data.code:
git add src/auth/login.ts

git commit -m "feat(auth): validate refresh token expiry before rotation"

git add src/auth/session.ts

git commit -m "feat(auth): extend session lifetime based on activity"

data.text: Branch Naming Conventions
Consistent branch names help teammates understand purpose at a glance. Most teams use a prefix system followed by a short description and optional ticket ID.

data.title: Branch Naming Examples
data.code:
# Long-lived integration branches
git checkout -b main

# Feature branch linked to issue 482
git checkout -b feature/482-refresh-token-rotation

# Hotfix for production incident
git checkout -b hotfix/519-auth-header-missing

data.text: Enforcing Branch Names with Hooks
Git hooks can reject branch names that do not match a regex pattern. A pre-commit or pre-push hook enforces naming without relying on memory.

data.title: Branch Name Hook
data.code:
#!/bin/bash
BRANCH=$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)
if [[ ! $BRANCH =~ ^(main|develop|feature|bugfix|hotfix|release|chore|docs)/ ]]; then
  echo "Branch name must start with a valid prefix."
  exit 1
fi

data.text: Git Flow Overview
Git Flow defines five branch types: main, develop, feature, release, and hotfix. Each has a clear lifecycle. Many teams adopt a simplified version.

cards.title: main
cards.description: Production-ready code only. Every commit is a release.

cards.title: develop
cards.description: Integration branch for features. Next release built from here.

cards.title: feature/*
cards.description: New work branched from develop and merged back.

data.text: Git Flow Release Workflow
The release branch is created when develop has enough features for the next version. Bug fixes specific to the release are committed here.

data.title: Git Flow Release Branch Pattern
data.code:
# Start from develop
git checkout -b release/v2.4.0 develop

# Bump version, update changelog, fix bugs
git commit -am "chore(release): bump version to 2.4.0"

# Merge back to main
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff release/v2.4.0

git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release v2.4.0"

# Merge back to develop
git checkout develop
git merge --no-ff release/v2.4.0

data.title: Merge with --no-ff
data.text: Using --no-ff preserves a visible merge commit, making it easy to identify when a release happened.
GitHub Flow
GitHub Flow is simpler. Main is always deployable. New work happens on short-lived topic branches, opened as pull requests and merged after review.

items: Main is always deployable
Branch from main for every change
Open a pull request early and often
Merge only after review and passing checks
Deploy immediately after merge

data.title: GitHub Flow Workflow
data.code:
git checkout -b feature/900-dark-mode-toggle main
# Work, commit, push
git push origin feature/900-dark-mode-toggle

# Open PR, review, fix CI, then merge

data.title: Choose the Right Model
data.text: Use Git Flow for scheduled release trains with parallel releases. Use GitHub Flow for continuous deployment.
Trunk-Based Development
Trunk-based development keeps everyone on a single branch. Feature flags hide incomplete work. Short-lived branches merge back quickly. This supports high-frequency releases.

items: Everyone commits directly to trunk or short-lived branches
Feature flags control incomplete functionality
Merge frequency is high, often multiple times per day
Requires robust CI and automated testing

data.title: Trunk-Based Feature Flag

data.text: Version Tags
Tags mark specific commits as release points. Annotated tags store metadata such as tagger name, date, and message. Lightweight tags are simple pointers. For releases, prefer annotated tags.

data.title: Tagging a Release
data.code:
git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release v2.4.0

- Add refresh token rotation
- Fix login redirect loop"

git push origin v2.4.0

data.title: Listing and Checking Out Tags
data.code:
git tag

git show v2.4.0

git checkout v2.4.0

data.text: Signed Tags
For security-sensitive projects, use signed tags. A signed tag includes a cryptographic signature that verifies the tag was created by a trusted key.

data.title: Creating a Signed Tag
data.code: git tag -s v2.4.0 -m "Release v2.4.0"

data.text: Changelog Generation
A changelog documents what changed between releases. Many teams generate it automatically from conventional commits.

data.title: Conventional Changelog Example
data.code:
# Changelog generated from git log

## [v2.4.0] - 2026-09-15
### feat
- add refresh token rotation
### fix
- resolve login redirect loop

Generated by conventional-changelog

data.text: Automated Changelog Tools
Tools such as semantic-release, standard-version, and release-it can automate the entire release process: bumping versions, generating changelogs, creating tags, and publishing packages.

items: Parse conventional commits to determine version bump
Generate a changelog from commit history
Create and push a Git tag
Publish to npm, PyPI, or other registries
Post release notes to GitHub or Slack

data.text: Hotfix Branches
A hotfix branch handles production emergencies. It branches from the tagged main commit, fixes the issue, and merges back to both main and develop.

data.title: Hotfix Workflow
data.code:
# Branch from the tagged release
git checkout -b hotfix/519-auth-header v2.4.0

# Fix and commit
git commit -am "fix(auth): include Authorization header in proxy requests"

# Merge to main and tag
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff hotfix/519-auth-header
git tag -a v2.4.1 -m "Hotfix v2.4.1"

# Merge to develop
git checkout develop
git merge --no-ff hotfix/519-auth-header

data.text: Release Automation
Automating releases reduces human error. Common automation includes running tests on the release branch, bumping versions, generating changelogs, publishing packages, and notifying stakeholders.

items: CI runs full test suite on the release branch
Version numbers are bumped automatically
Changelog is generated from commit history
Artifacts are published to package registries
Slack or email notifications are sent to the team

data.title: GitHub Actions Release Workflow
data.code:
name: Release
on:
  push:
    branches: [release/*]
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
      - run: npm run changelog

data.text: PR Description Templates
A well-written PR description sets reviewers up for success. Include motivation, approach, test instructions, and screenshots for UI changes.

data.title: PR Description Template
data.code:
## What does this PR do?
Brief description of the change.

## Related issues
Closes #123

## Motivation
Why is this change needed?

## Approach
How does the change work?

## Testing
1. Step one
2. Step two

## Screenshots
<optional>

data.text: Commit Linting
Tools like commitlint enforce conventional commit formats in CI. Developers get immediate feedback if a message does not meet the standard.

data.title: commitlint with Husky

data.text: Rebasing Feature Branches
Before merging a feature branch, rebase it onto the latest main. This produces a linear history and lets you resolve conflicts incrementally.

data.title: Rebasing onto Main
data.code:
git checkout feature/auth-refactor
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# If conflicts occur, fix them and continue
git add .
git rebase --continue

data.title: Never Rebase Public History
data.text: Only rebase branches that have not been shared with others. Rewriting commits on a remote forces collaborators to re-sync.
Squash Merge Strategy
Squash merging collapses all commits from a feature branch into a single commit on main. The main history stays clean while detailed history remains on the feature branch.

data.title: Squash Merge via CLI
data.code:
# Merge with squash
git checkout main
git merge --squash feature/482-refresh-token-rotation

git commit -m "feat(auth): add refresh token rotation"

data.title: Squash vs No-Squash
data.text: Squash when you want a clean main history. Merge normally when individual commits carry review value that should remain visible.
Release Branch Checklist

data.title: Release Branch Checklist
items: All feature branches intended for the release are merged
Version number is updated in package.json and config files
Changelog is reviewed and finalized
Smoke tests and regression suite pass
Documentation is updated for user-facing changes
Tag is created and pushed after merge to main

data.text: Comparing Git Flow and GitHub Flow

cards.title: Release Cadence
cards.description: Git Flow: scheduled releases. GitHub Flow: continuous deployment.

cards.title: Branch Complexity
cards.description: Git Flow: many long-lived branches. GitHub Flow: short-lived branches only.

cards.title: Best For
cards.description: Git Flow: versioned products. GitHub Flow: SaaS and web apps.

cards.title: Learning Curve
cards.description: Git Flow: higher. GitHub Flow: lower and easier to teach.

data.text: Common Pitfalls

items: Merging a release branch without merging fixes back to develop
Forgetting to delete stale branches after merging
Using lightweight tags for production releases
Leaving WIP commits on shared branches
Skipping code review because the release is urgent

data.title: Protect Your Branches
data.text: Enable branch protection rules on main and release branches. Require status checks, signed commits if your team uses GPG, and pull request reviews before merge.
Coordinating Releases Across Teams
In organizations with multiple teams, release branches can become coordination bottlenecks. Sync meetings, shared dependency versions, and explicit cut-off dates prevent last-minute surprises.

items: Publish a release calendar with freeze dates
Coordinate dependency upgrades across teams
Use a shared changelog or release notes document
Run a pre-release smoke test on a staging environment

data.text: Communicating Breaking Changes
A breaking change must be communicated clearly. Update the changelog with a BREAKING CHANGE footer, notify downstream consumers, and provide a migration guide.

data.title: Breaking Change Commit Message
data.code:
feat(api)!: remove legacy v1 authentication endpoint

The /api/v1/auth endpoint has been replaced by /api/v2/auth.
Clients must migrate before v2.4.0 ships.

BREAKING CHANGE: /api/v1/auth no longer accepts requests.
Migration guide: https://example.com/docs/migration-v2

data.text: Release Notes Best Practices

items: Group changes by type: added, changed, fixed, removed
Highlight breaking changes at the top
Include upgrade instructions
Link to relevant documentation and migration guides
Thank contributors for significant changes

data.text: Advanced Commit and Release Topics
This deeper pass covers commit message anatomy, history rewriting, tagging conventions, and release-branch mechanics in more detail.
Subject Line Best Practices
The subject line is the most visible part of a commit. Keep it under 50 characters so it displays correctly in git log --oneline and GitHub pull request lists.

items: Use imperative mood: 'add' not 'added' or 'adds'
Do not end the subject with a period
Capitalize the first word
Be specific: 'fix auth redirect loop' not 'fix bug'

data.text: The Body of a Commit Message
The body explains the motivation and context. It is especially important for non-obvious changes. Future readers should understand why the change was made, not just what changed.

data.title: Commit with Detailed Body
data.code:
fix(auth): resolve infinite redirect loop

The login endpoint was redirecting to itself when the session cookie was missing. This happened because the middleware checked for the session after issuing the redirect.

The fix reorders the middleware so the session check runs before the redirect logic. This ensures unauthenticated users receive the login page instead of being caught in a loop.

data.text: Footer Metadata
The footer can contain issue references, co-author credits, and breaking-change notices. Use it to link your work to tracking systems and to alert consumers of breaking changes.

data.title: Commit with Footer Metadata
data.code:
feat(api)!: remove legacy v1 endpoint

BREAKING CHANGE: The /api/v1/users endpoint has been removed. Use /api/v2/users instead. See migration guide at https://example.com/docs/migration.

Co-authored-by: Jane Doe <jane@example.com>

data.text: Splitting a Large Change into Multiple Commits
If you have been working for several days on a feature, you likely have a tangled set of changes. Use git add -p and git reset -p to stage only related hunks, creating a series of atomic commits.

data.title: Using git reset -p
data.code:
# Unstage a specific hunk
git reset -p src/auth/login.ts

# Stage only the login changes, leaving session changes unstaged

data.text: Rewriting History Before Pushing

Before pushing, review your local commit history with git log --oneline. If you see WIP commits, typos, or mixed changes, use git rebase -i to clean them up. A clean history before pushing reduces noise for reviewers.

data.title: Reviewing Local History
data.code:
git log --oneline -10

# Output:
# abc1234 feat(auth): add refresh token rotation
# def5678 fix(auth): resolve redirect loop
# ghi9012 chore: update dependencies

data.text: Cherry-Picking Commits
Cherry-picking applies a specific commit from one branch onto another. It is useful when you need a bug fix from a feature branch on main without merging the entire branch.

data.title: Cherry-Picking a Commit
data.code:
# On main, apply only the fix commit
git cherry-pick def5678

# If conflicts occur, resolve and continue
git cherry-pick --continue

data.text: Reverting Commits
Reverting creates a new commit that undoes the changes of a previous commit. Unlike resetting, reverting is safe on shared branches because it does not rewrite history.

data.title: Reverting a Commit
data.code:
git revert abc1234

# Opens editor for revert message
# Commit the revert

data.text: Reverting a Merge Commit
Reverting a merge commit requires specifying which parent to revert to. Use -m 1 to revert to the first parent, which is typically the branch you merged into.

data.title: Reverting a Merge
data.code: git revert -m 1 abc1234

data.text: Tagging Conventions
Teams often use tag prefixes to distinguish release types: v1.0.0 for stable releases, v1.0.0-rc.1 for release candidates, and v1.0.0-beta.1 for early testing.
Annotated vs Lightweight Tags
Annotated tags store metadata: tagger, date, and message. Lightweight tags are just pointers. Use annotated tags for releases so you have a record of who tagged and why.

data.title: Comparing Tag Types
data.code:
# Annotated tag
git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release v2.4.0"

# Lightweight tag
git tag v2.4.0

data.text: Signing Tags and Commits
For high-security environments, sign tags and commits with GPG. This ensures the tag or commit was created by a trusted key and has not been tampered with.

data.title: Signing a Commit
data.code: git commit -S -m "feat(auth): add refresh token rotation"

data.text: Release Branch Naming
Use clear, versioned names for release branches. Avoid generic names like 'release' because they do not indicate which version is being prepared.

items: Use release/v1.2.0, not just release
Keep release branches in the same repository
Delete release branches after merging to main and develop
Do not push feature commits to release branches

data.text: Hotfix vs Regular Release
Hotfixes are for critical production issues. They branch from a tagged main commit, not from develop. Regular release branches prepare planned versions from develop.

cards.title: Hotfix
cards.description: Branched from main tag. Emergency fix. Merged to main and develop.

cards.title: Release
cards.description: Branched from develop. Planned version. Merged to main and develop.

data.text: Release Freeze
A release freeze is a period during which no new features are added to a release branch. Only bug fixes and documentation updates are allowed. This stabilizes the release for testing and deployment.

items: Announce the freeze date in advance
Block feature PRs targeting the release branch
Allow only critical bug fixes during freeze
Run a final regression test before tagging

data.text: Release Notes Automation
Automate release notes generation from conventional commits. Tools like standard-version parse the commit history and produce a changelog without manual effort.

data.title: standard-version Configuration

data.text: Semantic Release
Semantic release fully automates versioning and publishing. It analyzes conventional commits, determines the next version, generates a changelog, creates a tag, and publishes to npm.

data.title: Semantic Release GitHub Action
data.code:
- uses: cycjimmy/semantic-release-action@v4
  with:
    extra_plugins:
      - '@semantic-release/changelog'
      - '@semantic-release/npm'
      - '@semantic-release/github'

data.text: Dependency Updates During Release
Update dependencies in a separate chore commit before the release branch is cut, or in a dedicated maintenance branch. Avoid mixing dependency bumps with feature commits on a release branch.

items: Run npm outdated or cargo outdated to check versions
Test the updated dependencies in a dedicated branch
Update package-lock.json or Cargo.lock alongside package.json
Document any migration steps required by major dependency bumps

data.text: Cross-Branch Synchronization
When you merge a release branch to main, also merge it to develop. This ensures bug fixes made on the release branch are not lost when the next release cycle starts on develop.

data.title: Synchronizing Release to Develop
data.code:
git checkout develop
git merge --no-ff release/v2.4.0

git push origin develop

data.text: Release Branch Regression Testing
Run the full regression suite on the release branch before tagging. Catching issues on the release branch is cheaper than catching them in production after the release has shipped.

items: Run unit, integration, and E2E tests
Perform manual exploratory testing on staging
Verify third-party integrations
Check monitoring and alerting dashboards

data.text: Rollback Procedures
If a release causes issues in production, rolling back should be fast. Tagged releases make it easy to deploy a previous version. Document the rollback procedure in your runbook.

data.title: Rollback Runbook
data.code:
1. Identify the last known good tag: git tag --sort=-version:refname | head -5
2. Deploy the tag: kubectl set image deployment/app app=image:tag
3. Verify health checks pass
4. Notify stakeholders

data.text: Post-Release Validation
After deploying a release, validate that the system is healthy. Check error rates, latency, feature flags, and user-reported issues. A quick smoke test catches problems before they affect many users.

items: Monitor error rates and latency dashboards
Verify feature flags are set correctly
Check that third-party integrations are healthy
Review user feedback channels for reports

data.text: Common Release Mistakes

items: Forgetting to merge the release branch back to develop
Deleting the release branch before merging to develop
Tagging the wrong commit
Not running the full test suite on the release branch
Skipping code review for the release commit

data.text: Continuous Delivery Considerations
In continuous delivery environments, releases happen frequently. The release branch may be short-lived or unnecessary. Instead, main is always deployable, and every merge is a potential release.

items: Every merge to main passes CI and can be deployed
Feature flags control incomplete work
Automated canary deployments catch issues early
Rollbacks are automated and fast

data.text: Git Hooks for Commit Quality
Git hooks can enforce commit message format, prevent large files, run linters, and block secrets. Husky is a popular tool for managing Git hooks in JavaScript projects.

data.title: Husky Configuration

data.text: Lint-Staged for Atomic Commits
Lint-staged runs linters on staged files only. This encourages developers to fix issues before committing, keeping the history clean and avoiding noisy commits that only fix lint errors.

data.title: Lint-Staged Configuration

data.text: Commit Message Templates
Provide a commit message template in .gitmessage.txt or through Git configuration. This helps developers remember the structure and include all necessary information.

data.title: Git Message Template
data.code:
# <type>(<scope>): <subject>
# |<----  Using a Maximum Of 50 Characters  ---->|
# 
# Explain why this change is being made
# |<----   Try To Limit Each Line to a Maximum Of 72 Characters   ---->|
# 
# Provide links or keys to any relevant tickets, articles or other resources
# 
# --- COMMIT END ---
# Type can be feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, chore, or revert
# Scope is optional

data.text: Enforcing Conventions in CI
Even with local hooks, CI should also validate commit messages. A second line of defense prevents bad commits from entering the shared history if a developer bypasses local hooks.

data.title: CI Commit Message Validation
data.code:
- name: Validate commit messages
  run: |
    git log --format=%B ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}..${{ github.sha }} | commitlint

data.text: Release Branch Communication

Communicate the release branch status to the whole team. Use a dedicated Slack channel, a GitHub project board, or a shared document to track what is included, what is blocked, and the expected ship date.

items: Post the release checklist in a shared channel
Update the project board with release tasks
Tag the release manager in blocking issues
Send a reminder 24 hours before the freeze

data.text: Summary
Strong commit hygiene and disciplined release branching reduce risk and improve collaboration. Atomic commits, descriptive messages, and automated release processes help teams ship confidently.

data.title: Key Takeaways
text: Write atomic commits with conventional messages
Use release branches for stabilization before shipping
Automate versioning, changelog, and release steps
Protect main and release branches with branch protection rules
